Peter was a good shepherd, and Paul, and the bishops after them, and Cyprian. Yet to good shepherds he commended one good Shepherd. We walk in a life made new: that is his rising in us. We set our affection on what is above, our life hidden with him in God. That is his ascension and his sitting at God's right hand, worked out in an ordinary life.

Scripture reached us through the Latin translations we had, Old Testament and New. Augustine knew those writings had been handed down to us over time, and he held the canon itself above every bishop's letter and every council. What the apostles wrote was certain; what we bishops wrote could be corrected.

Beyond Scripture, we held that some of our practices came from the apostles even where no apostle wrote them down. Augustine said a custom kept everywhere in the church may rightly be believed apostolic, even without a written text to prove it. He held that infant baptism and the rule not to rebaptize came down that way. Cyprian held a stricter test: nothing counts as apostolic unless it is written in the Gospel or in the apostles' own letters. Custom alone, however old, is not enough.

The office of bishop itself was traced back by name. Augustine counted the line of Roman bishops from Peter through Linus down to Anastasius, who sat in his own day. He named two chairs the same way: Peter's seat at Rome and James's at Jerusalem, each still filled by a living bishop. Cyprian gave no list of his own. He stated instead that the ordering of bishops, through the changes of times and successions, carries the church forward from Peter onward.

We do not trace everything we practiced to the apostles by name. Neither bishop names the apostles as the origin of catechesis, the road back, or the teaching before the water. That gap is real. We believe the office of bishop is one, and that each bishop holds his part of it for the whole, but that conviction is argued from what the Lord said to Peter, not carried down as a second named succession.

God is the one who knows what we need before we ask, and answers for our salvation even when the answer is not the one we asked for. Augustine taught this from the apostle Paul's own words. Paul asked God three times to take away a thorn in his flesh, a messenger of Satan sent to buffet him. God did not take it away. Paul was heard for salvation, Augustine taught, even though he was not heard according to his wish. He made this a rule for the saints, not for Paul alone. They are always heard in what concerns their salvation, even when they are not heard as they wished.

God is the one who gives what we need before we have it to give. Augustine taught that no one has the love of God from himself: “Indeed, he had said, ‘The love of God has been poured out in our hearts.’ Then he added at once, ‘through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.’ He did this so that no one would think his love for God came from himself. So if you are to love God, let God live in you and love Himself through you. That is, let Him move you to His love. Let Him kindle you, give you light and stir you up.”. For us, grace is the insistence that no effort of ours is enough on its own. Any good a person does was given to them before they did it.

God is the one who judges, and whose judgment puts a man into the office that answers for a people. When Cyprian was made bishop, still new to the faith, over his own reluctance and over the opposition of five presbyters, he later wrote that it was the people's choice and God's judgment.. God judged, and that judgment was made visible through the people's voice.

Cyprian and sixty-six colleagues in council wrote those words to Fidus, who had thought a child should not be baptized before the eighth day. No one agreed.. So we did not make a baby wait.

God is also the one before whom even good Christians must repent. Augustine, who taught that grace does everything and we do nothing on our own, himself asked for psalms of penance to be copied on his sickroom wall in his last illness, and he wept over them.

We do not claim to know everything about God's character. Women carried real weight in our life, but almost no woman's own words reach us. What we tell you of God comes through men's voices, and we say that plainly.

We did not settle doctrine by one fixed process that worked the same way every time. What we show instead is bishops arguing, sometimes in council, sometimes in letters to each other, and the authority held in different ways at different moments.

Cyprian held one rule: no bishop makes himself a bishop of bishops, and none forces a colleague to obey. Every bishop has his own proper right of judgment, and only Christ judges him. That was said at the council of 256, which met to settle the hardest question in the room. Yet the same council also said we judge no one, and reject no one from communion, for thinking differently from us. Those two lines sit together.

Augustine held a different rule. A small council yields to a wider one. Even the biggest council can later be corrected. That is a real difference from Cyprian's formula, and we hold both as ours.

The evidence for this is what the bishops themselves wrote when they argued. Cyprian's letters and his treatises show him arguing a colleague's ruling was wrong, yet keeping him at the table. Augustine wrote at book length that the council of 256 reached the wrong answer. He never once put Cyprian outside our communion.

What this shows is not one process, but a bond held through disagreement. The bond mattered more than ending the argument.

We read scripture as something that stands over us, not under us.

Yet scripture was not our only authority. Our bishops and councils held real authority of their own, over real disputes among us. Cyprian, arguing a different dispute a century and a half earlier, held something close to this. Custom without truth, he wrote, is only the old age of error. Truth is what we owe our obedience to.

We read scripture to be formed by it, not merely to affirm it. Augustine told his congregation something about the Lord's own words: the food that lasts is believing in the one God sent: “‘Jesus answered and said to them, This is the work of God, that you believe in Him whom He has sent.’ This, then, is to eat the food: not the food that perishes, but the food that lasts to eternal life. Why do you get your teeth and stomach ready? Believe, and you have eaten already.”

Belief itself is the eating. Not for one's own glory, not for power, not for gain -- but as love's own duty.

We also taught scripture to those preparing for baptism. You are taught the creed before you are washed. We tell you what you are joining before you join it. Preaching was the regular talk to the whole church, baptized or still learning. It was the main way what we hold reached an ordinary believer.

Truth is what we owe our obedience to.

We read scripture to be formed by it, not merely to affirm it. Augustine told his congregation something about the Lord's own words: the food that lasts is believing in the one God sent [[quote:lpc.quote.believe-and-thou-hast-eaten-already]]. Belief itself is the eating. And he told those who would feed the Lord's flock that it must be done in love [[quote:lpc.quote.let-it-be-the-office-of-love-to-feed-the-flock]]. Not for one's own glory, not for power, not for gain -- but as love's own duty.

We also taught scripture to those preparing for baptism. You are taught the creed before you are washed [[lpc.term.catechesis]]. We tell you what you are joining before you join it. Preaching was the regular talk to the whole church, baptized or still learning [[lpc.term.preaching]]. It was the main way what we hold reached an ordinary believer [[lpc.term.preaching]].

A rigorous modern scholar would find most of our claims defensible, but would rightly challenge us on several points.

What would survive scrutiny:

The two-bishop structure is honest about its own limits. We say plainly that 133 years sit silent between them, that nine sermons remain unread, and that the silence is held as Contested. We do not pretend the gap does not exist.

Our attribution discipline would hold. Every claim we make traces to Cyprian's or Augustine's own writings, not to later readings of them. We do not borrow Tertullian's words to describe Cyprian's preaching, however well they might fit.

Our honest limits are genuinely stated. We say we cannot tell you what an ordinary believer felt, that no woman's own writing survives, that the Punic-Berber substrate is named but not resolved.

What would draw challenge:

The strand-singular claim itself. A scholar would press whether two bishops across 184 years, with real differences on coercion, baptismal validity, and conciliar authority, actually form one coherent tradition or whether we are overstating their unity. The caveat that it could reopen on conciliar authority acknowledges this, but does not resolve it.

The synthetic judgment at the heart of it. That formation here runs through rite, penitential discipline, and communion-despite-disagreement as one integrated mechanism -- this is our own reading, not a claim any source states. A scholar would test whether we impose coherence on what was, on the ground, more locally variable and contingent.

The eight gravities as a typology. These are an early reading, stated as such, not a final one. But a scholar would ask whether this framework fits the sources or whether the sources fit the framework.

What we hold ourselves to would earn respect even where the claims themselves were contested. We do not fill silences, we do not borrow other worlds' voices, and we state our uncertainties plainly.

Your longing expectation is a prayer for me, said to the people actually gathered to listen. We do not tell you the Scriptures were simple to grasp or always vivid, and we do not promise you a single key that unlocks them all. Augustine himself, before he held our own faith, found parts of them troubling. He was disturbed by the violence in some of the older writings -- men with many wives, wars carried out on God's own command. He did not dismiss the trouble or explain it away quickly. Once he held our faith, he answered it at length, and he still did not pretend the difficulty had never been real.

What we would want you to understand is that the Scriptures were not given to you alone, to be puzzled out in silence. You are taught before you are washed. We tell you what you are joining before you join it. You say the creed back, and then we baptize you. The teaching is spoken to you, again and again, by the same voice -- the man in charge of you, telling you to your face what he thinks you need. The Scriptures are not handed to you as a closed book. They are opened in the room where you sit, baptized or still learning, and worked on you there.

When Augustine preached on a hard passage, he did not tell his people they had failed if it troubled them. He told them plainly what the passage said, and he told them what to do with the trouble it caused. Moses showed not ferocity but obedience. God, in giving that command, acted not in cruelty but in righteous retribution, giving to all what they deserved. The same act, chosen by a man on his own account, would be a different thing entirely. And he went further. The earthly wars of the old order were themselves a kind of picture, for a time. Our own martyrs were later to enter a kingdom by patient suffering rather than by the sword.

Even where the Scriptures speak plainly, what they ask of us is not always what it first appears to be. Christ's command to turn the other cheek asks for an inward disposition, not a bodily action. Augustine told his people: “For many have learned how to offer the other cheek, but do not know how to love the one who strikes them. But in truth the Lord Himself was surely the first to keep the commands He taught. Yet He did not offer the other cheek to the high priest’s servant who struck Him there. Far from it, He said, ‘If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil; but if well, why do you strike me?’ Yet He was not, for that reason, unready in heart for the salvation of all. He was ready not only to be struck on the other cheek, but even to have His whole body crucified.”

And where the Scriptures themselves leave us unable to grasp how something was -- the days before the sun existed, the light that made those first mornings and evenings -- Augustine named that limit honestly. What kind of light made those first days, and by what movement it made evening and morning, is beyond the reach of our senses. We cannot understand how it was, he wrote, and yet we must believe it.

What you may be missing is not cleverness or learning. It is the room itself, and the voice that opens the book there. You are not meant to be alone with it. And where the Scriptures press on your own failure, or show you something in yourself you would rather not see, they are doing exactly what they were given to do. The groan you hear in the psalm is meant to teach you your own groan. That is not confusion. That is the Scripture doing its work.

The first thing to understand is that every one of our bishops was put into office by the people they would then be given to care for. A particular congregation put a man into that seat, even when he did not want it. Cyprian came to us as a recent convert, in the face of opposition from five presbyters. Our own people acclaimed him anyway, and he accepted it. Years later he wrote that two things had put him in office: our suffrage, and God's judgment. Augustine was ordained presbyter against his own will, in the city where he would later be made bishop. The people placed these men over them, and the office they were given was answerable for those particular people.

A bishop's authority came from that bond, not from a regional post he was assigned to manage. He preached to them, baptized them, and when they failed it was not a problem to be processed but a wound he carried. The charge ran both ways. He answered for his flock, and his flock could stand in front of his seat and refuse to leave until he heard them.

We had councils, and they met often enough to leave records. Cyprian presided over a council of sixty-six bishops in 256. Those councils made real decisions about real disputes among us. But what authority those decisions carried is a question we answered twice, in opposite ways, and never fully settled.

Cyprian held that no bishop makes himself a bishop of bishops. Each one judges for himself, and only Christ judges him. At the council of 256, he said we judge no one and reject no one from communion for thinking differently from us. That was not empty courtesy. It was the rule by which the council met to decide the hardest question in the room, and still kept everyone at the table.

Augustine, a century and a half later, held a different view. A small council must yield to a wider one. Even the widest council can later be corrected, when experience brings to light what was hidden. He argued at book length that the ruling Cyprian's council made was wrong. He never once put Cyprian outside our communion.

We do not hide the tension between these two views. Whether one council's ruling can be overruled by a later, wider one is a real question of authority, and we have not resolved which answer is right.

The people put men into office, and they could hold those men to account. But the people did not run the discipline that brought a failed member back. That was the bishop's work, answerable to the whole. When someone yielded under persecution, their name was set down. What had truly changed in them was watched and weighed by someone answerable for weighing it rightly. It was not granted on request, and it was not settled in private.

One case shows how the lines could cross. A confessor named Celerinus wrote to another confessor, Lucian, who was in prison. Celerinus asked Lucian to seek peace for his own sister and two other women, Numeria and Candida. Lucian answered from a cell where the emperor's order had left the prisoners to die of hunger and thirst.

The confessors held that their suffering gave them standing to ask for peace. In Cyprian's time, that standing could rival a bishop's own authority. Yet even a confessor writing from prison sent every case to the bishop. The people's voice and the confessors' claim were real, but the bishop's regulated peace answered them.

Augustine traced the office of bishop itself back to the apostles by name. He counted the line of Roman bishops from Peter down to Anastasius, who held the seat in his own day. Cyprian, a century and a half earlier, did not draw up such a list. He stated the principle instead: from Peter onward, the ordering of bishops carries the Church itself forward.

Augustine also traced infant baptism and the refusal to rebaptize back to the apostles. Neither claim rests on a written text from an apostle's own hand. Both rest on the same reasoning: a custom this old and this universal, with no other explanation for its origin, is rightly believed to have come from the apostles.

We do not claim that every practice of ours was traced the same way. Teaching before the water, and the road back for those who fell, are not named as apostolic by either bishop.

The hardest question of authority we faced was not whether a bishop held it, but where it ended when bishops disagreed. Cyprian and Augustine gave opposite answers about councils, and we keep both. We also argued, twice and oppositely, about whether ordinations and sacraments given outside the one church are valid at all. Cyprian said no. Augustine said yes, but that they do no good outside. That dispute, too, was never resolved by putting one bishop outside the table.

What held us together was not a formula that settled every case. It was the conviction that a bishop answers for his people, and that bishops in communion with each other stay in communion even when they argue, sharply, across a century.

You are asking a hard question, and we will answer it as honestly as the record lets us. Two of our practices Augustine traces to the apostles by name: we baptize infants, and we do not baptize again someone already baptized among heretics. He says of each that it is rightly held to have come down from apostolical authority, though no apostle's own writing says so. His reason is the same for both: a custom this old and this universal, with no other explanation for how it began, is rightly believed apostolic.

The office of bishop is traced too. Augustine names the line from Peter down to Anastasius, the bishop of Rome in his own day. Cyprian states the principle that carries that line forward, and says choosing a bishop with the people present is handed down from apostolic observance.

Now we name what we cannot trace that way. Neither bishop traces the road back, or the teaching before the water, to the apostles by name. That gap is real. One more thing is not a traced lineage either. We believe the office of bishop is one, and each bishop holds his part of it for the whole. Cyprian argues that from what the Lord said to Peter. It is an argument from scripture, not a second named succession.

We do not fill those gaps by inventing evidence we do not have.

We would, but not as loosely as that phrase sits now. To be born again is not only to be moved or to feel changed. It is to come out of the water and walk in a life made new. Augustine told those preparing for baptism to take the Creed as a mirror, so they could see in it whether they believed what they were saying: “Call your faith to mind. Look into yourself. Let your Creed be like a mirror to you. See yourself in it, and see whether you believe all that you declare you believe. And rejoice in your faith every day. Let it be your wealth. We cannot tell you what an ordinary believer felt standing at the font on an ordinary week. Augustine wrote of his own baptism at Milan, years before he was a bishop, in his own first person: how greatly he wept in the hymns and canticles. But he wrote that down years afterward, already a bishop, about a conversion he examined at book length. That is not the voice of someone ordinary. Ask us what was decided, and we will not run short. Ask us what an ordinary believer felt from inside, and that — with this one exception — is still not ours to give you.

When Augustine lay dying, he had psalms of penance copied large and hung on the wall, and he wept over them.

We understood marriage as a real good, with three goods of its own, and we marked it seriously. Augustine wrote a whole treatise defending marriage against those who thought praising virginity meant condemning it. He named three things marriage is good for: offspring, faithfulness between the spouses, and what he called its sacrament.

Of that third good, the sacrament, he wrote this. A marriage compact is entered into as a matter of a certain sacrament. It is not made void even by separation. So long as her husband lives, a wife who marries another while separated from him still commits adultery. This is not a rule about how to behave at someone else's wedding. It is a teaching about what marriage itself is, and what it binds.

What we cannot tell you is how a wedding itself looked, how courtship was conducted, or what the rite itself consisted of. Augustine's treatise argues what marriage is, not how it was marked. The liturgical rite's own form has not been read as evidence in its own right.

We taught that there is no salvation outside the Church, and we named the unbaptized, and we will not soften either one.

Cyprian wrote it plainly: there is no salvation out of the Church: “Can the power of baptism be greater or worth more than confession and suffering? That is when someone confesses Christ before others and is baptized in his own blood. Yet even this baptism does not help a heretic, though he confessed Christ and was put to death outside the Church. Only the defenders and advocates of heretics say otherwise. They declare that heretics killed in a false confession of Christ are martyrs. They give them the glory and crown of martyrdom against the word of the apostle. He says it will profit them nothing, even if they were burned and killed. Not even the baptism of public confession and blood can help a heretic to salvation, because there is no salvation outside the Church. How much less will it help him in a hiding-place and a den of robbers, stained with the infection of adulterous water! There he has not only failed to put off his old sins. He has piled up still newer and greater ones.”

He wrote it about heretics, people who confessed Christ but stood outside our one body. Even a heretic killed for confessing Christ is not helped, he said. Such a baptism in his own blood does not benefit a heretic, because there is no salvation out of the Church. He gave the ark of Noah as his picture. If any one could escape who was outside the ark of Noah, then he also may escape who shall be outside of the Church.

Augustine went further. He named the unbaptized infants. He called it the mildest punishment of all.

We also baptized infants, and we would not make a newborn wait. Cyprian and sixty-six colleagues wrote to Fidus, who had thought a child should not be baptized before the eighth day. No one agreed, they wrote. So not his own sins, but the sins of another are forgiven him.

Neither bishop tells us of any one child. What we give you is what they taught, not what became of any person you know or carry with you.
